title: Northbridge Bank - Security review: retention controls + audit logs (Dedicated/Private)
summary: Northbridge Bank walked through their security review questions focused on data retention, audit logging, and evidence expectations for regulated workloads. Redwood clarified which data classes are in scope for retention controls (request/response logs where enabled, audit logs, traces/metrics, and certain artifacts), how default TTLs differ by Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and how purge jobs are enforced and verified. Northbridge emphasized need for (a) customer-configurable retention with minimum/maximum guardrails, (b) a clear legal hold / incident hold process, (c) audit-log export coverage including SSO/RBAC/admin actions, and (d) a customer-ready evidence package aligned to SOC 2 / ISO-style controls. Redwood committed to sending the retention controls overview + baseline compliance reporting pack outline, plus a sample audit-log export (redacted) and a list of audit event types currently covered. Next steps include a follow-up deep dive on Private deployment data residency + KMS integration and confirming target retention periods for Northbridge's intended deployment mode.
topics: Data classes and what Redwood stores vs does not store by default
Default retention by tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and customer overrides
Purge semantics (TTL enforcement, backfills, idempotency, verification metrics)
Legal hold and incident-response exceptions / break-glass access
Audit log coverage (event types, actor attribution, RBAC, SSO/SAML) and export formats
Baseline compliance reporting pack (retention export, audit log coverage summary, evidence checklist)
Data residency / region summary for Dedicated and Private
questions: Do you store prompts and completions by default, and can we turn off request/response logging entirely?
What are the minimum and maximum retention periods allowed, and can they vary by environment/region?
How do you prove deletion (purge verification) and what happens if purge jobs fall behind?
What is the legal hold process, who can approve it, and is it audited?
Which audit events are captured (policy changes, login, role changes, key management, export actions)?
Can we get time-windowed audit exports and a customer-ready evidence package for quarterly reviews?
action_items: Markus Klein - Send Northbridge the customer-facing retention controls overview + Security FAQ excerpts covering retention/audit logs (redacted where needed) - Due 2025-02-07
Olga Petrov - Share baseline compliance reporting pack outline and evidence checklist (SOC 2/ISO-style mapping) and confirm which sections are customer-ready for Q1 - Due 2025-02-10
Kevin Osei - Provide a sample audit-log export (CSV/JSON) with time-window filter and list of audit event types currently included; include notes on any known gaps - Due 2025-02-12
Marcus Lin - Confirm legal hold / incident hold workflow details (approvals, audit trail) and send short written summary suitable for vendor risk questionnaire - Due 2025-02-11

Northbridge (Erin Caldwell) - Send Northbridge’s target retention requirements by data class (audit logs, request logs, traces/metrics) and any regulatory constraints (e.g., 90 days vs 1 year) - Due 2025-02-13
Northbridge (Miguel Alvarez) - Confirm preferred deployment path (Dedicated vs Private in VPC) and required regions/data residency constraints - Due 2025-02-13
next_steps: Redwood to send retention + audit logging collateral and sample exports for Northbridge vendor risk review.
Schedule a 45-min technical deep dive on Private deployment: data residency, KMS/HSM, and where logs live (customer-managed vs Redwood-managed).
Northbridge to provide target retention durations by data class; Redwood to confirm feasibility/guardrails by tier.
Follow-up on audit log event-type coverage and any roadmap items needed for Northbridge’s checklist.
transcript:
Meeting: Northbridge Bank - Security review: retention controls + audit logs (Dedicated/Private)
Recorded: 2025-02-06 14:03 ET
Duration: 53 min

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering, host), Marcus Lin (Security Engineering), Olga Petrov (GRC), Kevin Osei (Engineering - audit exports/retention)
- Northbridge Bank: Erin Caldwell (Vendor Risk), Priyanka Shah (InfoSec/GRC), Miguel Alvarez (Cloud Platform), Hannah Wu (Security Architect), Tom Becker (Procurement)

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed retention controls by data class, default TTLs, and customer-configurable policies.
- Reviewed audit log coverage, exporter capabilities, and evidence expectations.
- Confirmed need for customer-ready compliance reporting pack and deletion verification.

Topics
1) What data is stored and where
2) Retention configuration + enforcement
3) Legal hold / incident exceptions
4) Audit logs: event types + export
5) Evidence package / compliance report pack
6) Next steps and timeline

Action items
- Redwood to send retention controls overview and FAQ answers.
- Redwood to send sample audit export and list of event types.
- Redwood to send compliance reporting pack outline / evidence checklist.
- Northbridge to confirm target retention requirements and deployment mode.

Transcript
[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Markus from Redwood. This call is focused on retention controls and audit logging, and what evidence you all need for the vendor risk package. We’ve got Marcus from Security, Olga from GRC, and Kevin who’s been working on the audit export bits.

[00:19] Erin Caldwell: Great. Thanks Markus. Just to level set, we’re early-ish but this is a blocker. We need to understand retention by data type, whether you can do shorter TTLs, and what the audit logs look like. Also we’ll need something we can attach to our SOC 2 aligned questionnaire.

[00:36] Priyanka Shah: Yeah, and we’re looking at Dedicated or Private, not the public shared thing. We have some residency requirements too.

[00:46] Markus Klein: Makes sense. We’ll cover Dedicated and Private. Quick intros? Erin you already did. Miguel, Hannah, Tom?

[00:54] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel, platform engineering. I’ll ask the “where does it run and where do logs go” questions.

[01:01] Hannah Wu: Hannah, security architect. I’m focused on audit coverage, admin actions, RBAC, SSO, that stuff.

[01:08] Tom Becker: Tom, procurement. I’ll mostly listen and then ask about deliverables and timelines.

[01:14] Markus Klein: Great. I’ll start with a quick framing then we’ll go Q&A. So, retention controls: the product direction is customer-configurable retention across key data classes: request/response logs (if enabled), audit logs, traces/metrics, and artifacts like evaluation datasets if you’re using them in the console. For Private, depending on architecture, some of that is in your VPC or on-prem, and you control storage. For Dedicated, it’s Redwood-managed infra but isolated.

[01:43] Erin Caldwell: When you say request/response logs, do you mean you store the prompt and completion?

[01:49] Marcus Lin: It depends on configuration. By default, we do not persist full prompt/completion content for Hosted API except in limited debugging modes, and those are time-bound. For Dedicated and Private, we can configure request logging levels. You can disable request/response logging entirely, or store metadata only, like route, model, latency, tokens, and error codes. If content logging is enabled, it’s treated as a separate data class with strict TTL.

[02:17] Priyanka Shah: Okay. We need an explicit answer we can paste: “can be disabled,” “metadata only,” and “retention is X.”

[02:26] Olga Petrov: We can provide that in writing. We’ve been standardizing the language for questionnaire responses so it’s consistent: what’s stored by default, what’s optional, and what controls exist.

[02:39] Hannah Wu: For audit logs, what’s the retention default? Our internal standard for some systems is 365 days for audit trails, but for app logs we often want 30 or 90.

[02:50] Kevin Osei: Audit logs have a different default than request logs. Typically we keep audit longer, and we set min/max bounds by tier. I don’t want to quote exact numbers offhand because it depends on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, but the pattern is: audit logs longer, request logs shorter, traces/metrics somewhere in between.

[03:11] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Mechanically, how does TTL enforcement happen? Is it a database TTL, or a job, or…?

[03:18] Kevin Osei: It’s enforced with scheduled purge jobs per data store. Some stores support native TTL indexes, some are job-based deletes. The important parts: deletions are idempotent, batched to avoid DB pressure, and we emit verification metrics like “ttl lag seconds” and “rows deleted” and failures.

[03:39] Hannah Wu: I want to dig into “prove deletion.” We get asked by audit, “how do you validate records are actually removed at end of retention?”

[03:47] Marcus Lin: Great question. We do a couple things: we log the purge job execution and we track lag between record age and deletion time. Additionally, we can do periodic sampling checks, like querying for records older than retention and ensuring the count is zero or within a small tolerated window while jobs catch up. For Private deployments, you can also validate in your own logging backend since it’s your storage.

[04:15] Erin Caldwell: You said “tolerated window.” That’s a phrase that sometimes causes problems. What’s the SLA there?

[04:21] Markus Klein: Yeah, fair. The deletion is best-effort within the enforcement interval. We typically express it as “purge runs at least daily” and “maximum lag” with alerting. For regulated customers we can commit to tighter operational targets in Dedicated/Private. We should give you the exact language we use.

[04:42] Tom Becker: And will that language be in the compliance pack you’re building? Or is that separate?

[04:47] Olga Petrov: The baseline compliance reporting pack includes: retention configuration export (what TTL is set per data class), audit log coverage summary, data residency summary, RBAC/access controls report, and an evidence checklist. It won’t be a custom SLA doc by itself, but it will include the evidence that controls exist and are configured as agreed.

[05:12] Priyanka Shah: Can you show us an example of the “retention configuration export”? Like what fields are in it.

[05:18] Kevin Osei: We can send an example JSON export. It includes policy version, effective date, who changed it, and TTL per data class. It also includes exceptions like “legal hold enabled” or “logging disabled,” and it references the scope—tenant, environment, and region if applicable.

[05:41] Miguel Alvarez: Region-specific retention matters for us because we might run us-east and eu-west. Is that supported?

[05:48] Kevin Osei: The schema supports per-region overrides, yes, with guardrails so you don’t accidentally set conflicting policies. There’s a precedence model: tenant default, then environment, then region overrides. Policy changes are audited.

[06:06] Hannah Wu: Can you define the data classes? Because sometimes vendors call everything “audit log.” We separate “security audit logs” from “application request logs.”

[06:16] Marcus Lin: Same. We define “audit logs” as security/admin events: authentication events, console access, API key creation/rotation, role changes, retention policy changes, export actions, and similar. “Request logs” are request/response metadata and optionally content if enabled. “Telemetry” is traces/metrics used for performance monitoring. Artifacts are things like evaluation datasets, if you upload them.

[06:45] Erin Caldwell: Do you store customer payloads in traces?

[06:48] Markus Klein: Generally no. Traces are metadata—timings, route names, status, and request IDs. We avoid putting prompt content into trace spans. If there’s an exception, it’s documented and would be under the same logging controls.

[07:06] Priyanka Shah: We also need legal hold. If there is an investigation, can you stop deletion?

[07:12] Marcus Lin: Yes. There are two concepts: legal hold and incident hold. Legal hold is a formal process—requires approval from Security and Legal, and it’s auditable. Incident hold is short-term for production incidents, also auditable, and time-bounded. Both prevent purge for the scoped data classes and time ranges.

[07:36] Hannah Wu: Who can activate it? That’s usually the crux.

[07:40] Marcus Lin: Not an individual engineer. It’s restricted. For legal hold, it’s CISO delegate plus Legal approval, and it creates an audit event. For incident hold, it’s on-call lead plus Security approval, and it also creates an audit event and an expiration time.

[08:01] Erin Caldwell: We’ll need that in writing too.

[08:04] Olga Petrov: Understood.

[08:07] Miguel Alvarez: On Private deployment, are those purge jobs running in our environment?

[08:13] Markus Klein: For Private, yes—generally the data plane is in your network boundary. The control plane can be private as well. The purge framework runs as part of the deployment; you can monitor it and integrate with your observability. Redwood provides the job definitions, dashboards, and runbooks.

[08:32] Miguel Alvarez: Does it require specific backing services? Like Postgres vs ClickHouse.

[08:36] Kevin Osei: It depends on which stores you deploy. For audit logs and request logs, there’s a supported set. We’ll outline the prerequisites in the Private installer docs. The key is: whatever store is used must support TTL enforcement via native TTL or scheduled deletions.

[08:55] Hannah Wu: Audit event types. Can you list them? We need to know whether “role change,” “SSO config change,” “token creation,” “export performed,” are captured.

[09:05] Kevin Osei: High-level yes to those. We have a catalog of event types. Off the top: user login/logout, SSO/SAML config changes, API key create/rotate/revoke, RBAC role create/update/delete, policy changes (including retention policy), admin actions in the console, and audit export generation/download.

[09:28] Priyanka Shah: What about data plane access? Like if a Redwood SRE accesses a host.

[09:34] Marcus Lin: For Dedicated, privileged access is tightly controlled, logged, and requires ticketed approval. Some of that is captured as operational audit events. For Private, your team controls the infrastructure access, so those events are in your own IAM and host logging.

[09:55] Erin Caldwell: I’m going to be blunt: we get dinged when audit logs are “partial.” Are there known gaps?

[10:02] Kevin Osei: There are always edge cases. For example, some older admin actions weren’t emitting events historically; we’ve been closing those. Also, exporter filters sometimes omitted certain event types—there was a known issue we fixed recently. I’ll provide the current coverage list and note anything “planned” vs “GA.”

[10:27] Markus Klein: And to be clear, we’ll include that in the audit-log coverage summary in the compliance pack, so it’s explicit.

[10:35] Tom Becker: On exports: our audit team wants a time window export, like “Jan 1 to Jan 31,” and also filters by actor sometimes.

[10:43] Kevin Osei: That’s supported. The exporter can do time-windowed exports, filters by actor, event type, and tenant/environment. Output is CSV and JSON today, and we can bundle it into an evidence package.

[11:02] Hannah Wu: Evidence package: what does “bundle” mean? Like a zip file?

[11:07] Olga Petrov: Exactly. A customer-ready package that includes: retention config export, audit log export for a time window, and a README describing how it was generated, plus an evidence checklist. For some customers we also include screenshots from the console showing the retention settings page and RBAC.

[11:29] Erin Caldwell: That would help. We’re trying to avoid five different PDFs.

[11:33] Markus Klein: Yup, that’s the goal.

[11:37] Miguel Alvarez: One more: Do you have data residency reporting? We need to show “data stored in US only” for some environments.

[11:44] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, we can pin region and provide a region summary. For Private, it’s your environment, so residency is determined by where you deploy. The compliance pack includes a data residency summary section—regions configured, and which services are region-scoped.

[12:05] Priyanka Shah: Our questionnaire also asks about retention of metrics and traces, and whether logs go to third parties.

[12:12] Marcus Lin: In Hosted/Dedicated, there are sub-processors for telemetry depending on configuration, but we can provide the list and whether the data includes customer content. For regulated customers, we can route telemetry to a customer-managed sink or restrict it. For Private, again, it’s typically in your own observability stack.

[12:34] Hannah Wu: Okay. Let’s talk about defaults and guardrails. Can customers set retention to “0”?

[12:40] Kevin Osei: For some classes, yes—meaning disabled storage. For audit logs, typically we don’t allow “zero,” because you need auditability. But we can set a minimum, like 30 days or 90 days, depending on tier and requirements. For request logs, you can disable content and keep metadata only.

[13:02] Erin Caldwell: That’s acceptable. But we need it clearly stated. We’ve had vendors say “configurable” and then it’s not.

[13:10] Markus Klein: Understood. We’ll send the concrete min/max ranges we support for Dedicated and Private.

[13:17] Miguel Alvarez: Another technical: purge semantics. If I reduce retention from 365 to 30, does it back-delete older data?

[13:25] Kevin Osei: Yes, there’s a backfill behavior. When a policy becomes stricter, purge jobs will delete records older than the new threshold. It’s still batched, and we watch for backlog. When a policy becomes less strict, we obviously can’t resurrect data, but we will keep future data longer.

[13:50] Hannah Wu: And that policy change is audited?

[13:52] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy changes generate audit events and we keep a change history: who, when, what changed.

[14:03] Priyanka Shah: If an admin changes retention in the console, is that logged too? Not just via API.

[14:08] Kevin Osei: Yes. Console actions go through the same control plane and create audit events.

[14:17] Erin Caldwell: How many admins at Redwood can change retention on our behalf?

[14:22] Marcus Lin: In Dedicated, we aim for customer-managed configuration. Redwood can assist under a support workflow, but it’s controlled and auditable, and we can restrict it further contractually. In Private, Redwood doesn’t have access unless you explicitly grant it.

[14:43] Tom Becker: That’s going to come up in contracting. We’ll handle later.

[14:46] Markus Klein: Cool. I want to make sure we answer evidence expectations. Erin, what do you need as outputs for the review?

[14:53] Erin Caldwell: Three things: 1) written retention policy capability statement, 2) sample audit logs with event types, and 3) a checklist / mapping for SOC 2 style controls. Also, if you have SOC 2 report, we’ll request under NDA.

[15:10] Olga Petrov: We can do that. The baseline pack is meant to cover (1) and (3). For (2) Kevin can provide a sanitized export.

[15:20] Hannah Wu: For the audit export: do you include the actor identity? Like email or ID.

[15:26] Kevin Osei: Yes—actor ID, actor type (user/service), source IP when available, user agent, action, target resource, timestamp, and outcome. If SSO is configured, it maps to the SSO subject.

[15:46] Miguel Alvarez: Does it include request IDs to tie to app logs?

[15:49] Kevin Osei: Some events include correlation IDs. Request logs have request IDs; audit logs have event IDs; there’s a relationship when the action triggers a data plane request (e.g., export generation). We can walk through it.

[16:10] Priyanka Shah: What about key management, KMS? If we use customer-managed keys, does key rotation show up in audit logs?

[16:18] Marcus Lin: Key configuration changes and rotations in our system are audited. For Private, your KMS logs are in your cloud provider and you can merge them into your SIEM.

[16:34] Hannah Wu: Okay. Switching gears: what about the actual content in the compliance pack. Is it “on-demand”? Like we click a button.

[16:42] Markus Klein: The goal is on-demand generation in the console. In the short term, for early customers, we can generate it via internal tooling and deliver it securely. For GA it’ll be self-serve or support-assisted depending on tier.

[17:00] Erin Caldwell: We’re okay with support-assisted as long as it’s timely. What is “timely”? We have procurement timelines.

[17:07] Olga Petrov: For early stage, we’ve been targeting 3-5 business days for a full package including evidence attachments. Once the generator is fully productized, it should be same-day.

[17:21] Tom Becker: Please send that as a commitment you can stand behind. Otherwise we can’t plan.

[17:25] Markus Klein: We’ll send a “current process” timeline and what will be available by the time you’re in contracting.

[17:33] Miguel Alvarez: I want to understand: for Dedicated, are logs stored in your systems or can they be shipped to ours?

[17:39] Markus Klein: Both. There’s default storage in Redwood-managed systems with retention controls, and we can also support forwarding/export to customer-managed SIEM/log bucket depending on integration.

[17:55] Hannah Wu: Do you support “write once read many” style storage?

[17:59] Marcus Lin: For Private, you can implement WORM in your storage layer. For Dedicated, we don’t claim WORM by default, but we can provide integrity controls, access logs, and export. If WORM is required, we’d likely recommend Private with customer-managed storage.

[18:22] Priyanka Shah: That’s helpful; we can route that accordingly.

[18:26] Erin Caldwell: What about deletion exceptions? For example, if there is a billing dispute or operational incident, do you keep logs beyond retention?

[18:34] Marcus Lin: Not by default. The only reasons to extend beyond configured retention would be a documented hold: legal hold or incident hold, both auditable, scoped, and time-bound. Otherwise purge continues.

[18:53] Hannah Wu: And is the hold scoped per data class? Like hold audit logs but not request logs.

[18:58] Marcus Lin: Yes, it can be scoped.

[19:02] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[19:04] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about your target retention periods. You said 365 for audit. Any specific requirements for request logs or traces?

[19:12] Erin Caldwell: For request logs, we prefer minimal. Ideally metadata only, 30 days. For anything with customer content, we want it off, or at most 7 days for break/fix.

[19:26] Hannah Wu: Traces/metrics can be 30-90 days, but we need to know if they can leak content.

[19:32] Marcus Lin: Our standard posture is no content in traces. Request content logging can be turned off. We can document how we prevent that and where exceptions might exist.

[19:46] Priyanka Shah: For audit, we’ll likely ask 365. If your max is less, that’s a problem.

[19:52] Kevin Osei: For Dedicated/Private, longer audit retention is generally supported. The limit is usually storage sizing and performance; we can set guardrails but 365 is a common ask.

[20:05] Miguel Alvarez: If you’re doing continuous batching or KV cache, does that impact what’s logged? Sorry, I’m mixing performance and logging.

[20:12] Markus Klein: No worries. KV cache is in-memory; it’s not something we persist to logs. Performance optimizations don’t change retention. The logging pipeline is separate.

[20:26] Hannah Wu: Another audit question: do you log failed login attempts and lockouts?

[20:31] Kevin Osei: Yes, authentication events include failures. If you’re using SSO, some of that is in your IdP logs as well.

[20:42] Priyanka Shah: Do you support SCIM provisioning? And does that show up in audit logs?

[20:47] Markus Klein: SCIM is supported for enterprise tiers. Provisioning events are audited.

[20:55] Erin Caldwell: Great.

[20:57] Markus Klein: Any other big gaps we should address?

[21:01] Tom Becker: I’d like clarity on what you can deliver now vs roadmap. If you say “on-demand report pack,” but it’s not ready, we need a plan.

[21:11] Olga Petrov: Totally. For February, we can deliver: retention configuration export, audit log export (time-windowed), and an evidence checklist + narrative. The fully productized “click to generate” pack is in progress; we’ll share expected dates separately.

[21:33] Erin Caldwell: Okay. That might be enough for this cycle.

[21:37] Miguel Alvarez: If you’re Private, can we integrate the purge verification metrics into Prometheus?

[21:43] Kevin Osei: Yes, we emit metrics that can be scraped. We have dashboards for “ttl lag” and “purge errors” and backlog size.

[21:55] Hannah Wu: And alerts? Like if purge fails.

[21:58] Kevin Osei: Yes—alerts for sustained failures and lag above threshold.

[22:06] Marcus Lin: And from a control perspective, those alerts and runbooks are part of “monitoring” evidence.

[22:13] Priyanka Shah: That’s good.

[22:16] Erin Caldwell: I want to go back to “disable logging.” If we disable request/response logging, can your support still troubleshoot?

[22:23] Markus Klein: Good point. We can troubleshoot with metrics and traces that don’t include content. If deeper debugging is needed, we can do a time-bounded “debug mode” with explicit approval, and it’s auditable. But default is minimal.

[22:40] Hannah Wu: And that debug mode is a type of exception/hold?

[22:44] Marcus Lin: It’s an exception workflow, yes. It’s logged and time-bounded. It’s not a “hold,” it’s more like “temporarily increase logging.”

[22:55] Erin Caldwell: That’s acceptable if controlled.

[22:58] Miguel Alvarez: For Dedicated, do you have separate retention by environment? Like prod vs staging.

[23:03] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy can be scoped per environment, and you can set different TTLs.

[23:10] Priyanka Shah: Okay.

[23:12] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick run through the evidence artifacts we will send.

[23:17] Markus Klein: 1) Retention controls overview: data classes, defaults, configurable range, semantics.
2) Legal hold / incident hold write-up.
3) Audit log event type list + sample export.
4) Compliance reporting pack outline and checklist.

[23:39] Erin Caldwell: Add “data residency summary” please.

[23:41] Markus Klein: Will do.

[23:44] Hannah Wu: For the sample export, please include a retention policy change event, if possible, because that’s a key control.

[23:52] Kevin Osei: Yep, we can include that in the sample.

[23:56] Tom Becker: And what’s the secure channel for sending? Email is sometimes a problem.

[24:01] Olga Petrov: We can use our secure file share link with expiration, or upload to your portal if you have one.

[24:09] Erin Caldwell: We have a portal; I’ll send access.

[24:12] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[24:14] Miguel Alvarez: Any constraints on retention settings that might block us? Like minimum 30 days for audit? we might be okay, but I want to know.

[24:22] Kevin Osei: The main constraints are: audit logs cannot be turned off and have a minimum retention; request content logging can be disabled; and we enforce maximums to prevent unbounded storage in Hosted. For Dedicated/Private, maxima are higher and can be tuned.

[24:44] Priyanka Shah: Okay.

[24:46] Hannah Wu: Are exports immutable? Could an admin edit audit logs?

[24:51] Marcus Lin: Audit logs are append-only in storage; access is controlled. Exported files can be tampered with like any file, but we can provide checksums, and the integrity of underlying logs is protected by permissions and monitoring.

[25:08] Hannah Wu: Checksums would help.

[25:10] Kevin Osei: We can add a checksum file in the package.

[25:14] Markus Klein: Great call.

[25:16] Erin Caldwell: Also, if you do purge, do you purge in backups? This comes up.

[25:22] Marcus Lin: Backups have their own retention. For Hosted/Dedicated, we have backup retention policies and we can document them. In general, backups age out; we don’t do per-record deletion from backups in the short term, but backups expire within a defined window. For Private, backup retention is customer-controlled.

[25:46] Priyanka Shah: That’s important. We’ll need exact backup retention windows.

[25:52] Olga Petrov: We can provide our standard backup retention statement for the relevant tier.

[25:57] Tom Becker: Please do.

[26:00] Miguel Alvarez: For Private, if everything is in our VPC, do you still generate the compliance pack?

[26:06] Markus Klein: We can generate a pack that reflects your config and the product controls, but some evidence (like infrastructure access logs) will be yours. The pack will be a combination: Redwood-provided evidence + customer-provided evidence in the checklist.

[26:23] Erin Caldwell: That’s fine.

[26:25] Hannah Wu: What about redaction? If you give us a sample export, we don’t want real customer names.

[26:30] Kevin Osei: We’ll sanitize. Sample will be from an internal sandbox tenant with fake users.

[26:36] Markus Klein: We’re at about halfway. Any other questions we haven’t hit?

[26:42] Priyanka Shah: Just one: can retention be set by API? We prefer IaC.

[26:47] Kevin Osei: Yes, there are APIs, and for Private we have Terraform modules in progress. If you want day one, API-based config works.

[27:01] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[27:03] Hannah Wu: RBAC report—what is that?

[27:06] Olga Petrov: It’s basically a snapshot of roles and permissions: who has admin, who can export audit logs, who can change retention, and how those map to least privilege. It’s part of evidence.

[27:20] Erin Caldwell: Nice.

[27:22] Tom Becker: And is SSO required for that? We’ll require it.

[27:26] Markus Klein: For enterprise yes, we support SSO/SAML and we recommend it. We can make it a requirement in your tenant config.

[27:35] Marcus Lin: And audit logs will show SSO configuration changes.

[27:40] Hannah Wu: Perfect.

[27:43] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick recap then align on next meeting.

[27:48] Markus Klein: Recap: Redwood supports customer-configurable retention by data class with guardrails; request/response content logging can be disabled; audit logs are separate with longer retention. Purge is enforced via jobs with verification metrics and alerts. Legal hold and incident holds exist and are auditable. Audit logs include key admin/security events and can be exported with time windows and filters. We’ll provide a customer-ready evidence package.

[28:18] Erin Caldwell: Sounds right.

[28:20] Markus Klein: Next steps: We’ll send docs tomorrow, and we’ll schedule a Private deployment deep dive. Miguel, do you want to do that next week?

[28:28] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, Tuesday or Wednesday.

[28:31] Markus Klein: Erin, can you send your target retention requirements by data class? You already gave some verbally but we need it written.

[28:39] Erin Caldwell: Yes, I’ll send by end of next week.
